body.flop_note: Per element of x. Pass 1: v*v then accumulate (2). Pass 2: xv*gv then *rms (2). The 256-wide block reduction and one rsqrtf per row are 0.03 flop/element and are not counted.

notes: rse-hpc-lab/exercises/01-fused-rmsnorm rmsnorm_fused_block, DRAM regime N=2048 D=8192.

THE JUDGEMENT CALL THIS CASE EXISTS TO SETTLE: the kernel reads x twice — once for the sum of squares, once to normalise. The accounting declares ONE dram read, claiming the second is served by L2. gamma is D=8192 floats read by every block; at dram it is 32 KiB once, hence 0.00195 bytes/element.

MEASURED 2026-09-14, ncu 2025.3.1, RTX 5060 Ti, grid 2048 x block 256: lts__t_bytes.sum = 214,566,432 B = 12.79 B/element, which is x read TWICE plus y written once. The L2 claim is confirmed: the second pass never reaches the memory controller.

THE FINDING. Same launch, dram__bytes.sum = 118,885,888 B = 7.086 B/element, 0.886x the counted 8. Exercise 01 reports 385.71 GB/s for this kernel by dividing its 128 MiB analytic working set by 348.06 us. Measured traffic gives 341.57 GB/s. The headline is overstated by 12.9% because it counts bytes instead of measuring them -- and 385.71 is 107.6% of this machine's own measured reference bandwidth (358.43 GB/s), which is the tell that should have stopped it.
known_limits: [KNOWN LIMIT] gamma at L2 is not modelled. Every one of the 2048 blocks reads all 32 KiB of it, which would be 4 B/element of L2 traffic, yet total L2 is 12.79 B/element — so it is largely served below L2. This accounting makes no claim about L1 or constant cache.
[KNOWN LIMIT] One launch inside a repeated timing loop over the same 128 MiB buffers. Cache carry-over between iterations is part of what is measured here; a cold single pass is not.

[KNOWN LIMIT] `385.71 is above peak` is NOT established. The 358.43 GB/s reference is itself a lower bound (a torch.sum reduction, clocks unlocked) and the card's spec figure is 448 GB/s, so 385.71 is not physically impossible. What is established is narrower and enough: the kernel moves 12.9% fewer bytes than the headline divides by.
